source.title: Indian Polity (question set written from its topics)

chapter.name: Making of the Constitution
chapter.blurb: The demand for a Constituent Assembly, its composition and working, committees, enactment, enforcement and criticism.

concepts.name: Table 2.1 and 2.2: seat allocation and 1946 election results
concepts.description: Seats by area in the 1946 Assembly and the party-wise election results.
concepts.idea: The Assembly had 389 seats and the Congress won 208 of the 296 British Indian seats.
concepts.rule: Table 2.1: British Indian provinces (11) 292 seats, princely states 93 seats, Chief Commissioners' provinces (4) 4 seats, total 389. Table 2.2 (July-August 1946, 296 seats): Congress 208, Muslim League 73, Unionist Party 1, Unionist Muslims 1, Unionist Scheduled Castes 1, Krishak-Praja Party 1, Scheduled Castes Federation 1, Sikhs (non-Congress) 1, Communist Party 1, Independents 8.

questions.a: The eleven governor's provinces of British India

questions.a: Unionist Party, Unionist Muslims, Unionist Scheduled Castes, Krishak-Praja Party, SC Federation, Sikhs (non-Congress) and Communist Party win 1 each, which is 7 seats.

questions.q: Explain why 296 rather than 389 seats were contested in July-August 1946.
questions.a: Only the 296 seats of British India were elected; the 93 princely-state seats were not filled as the states stayed away.

questions.q: Which fraction of the 296 seats did the Congress win, approximately?
questions.a: About 70 per cent

questions.q: Show how the Congress and League results in Table 2.2 reflect the political situation of 1946.
questions.a: The Congress won the large majority of seats and the League most of the Muslim seats, so the two parties dominated, while other groups had few seats.

questions.a: Princely states had about a quarter of the seats

questions.q: Compare the seat share of British India and the princely states.
questions.a: British India had 296 of 389 seats and the princely states 93, so about three-fourths against one-fourth.

questions.q: Why did the absence of the princely states' representatives affect the Assembly's character at first?
questions.a: One-fourth of the seats were empty, so the Assembly initially represented British India only and had to wait for states to join later.

questions.q: Did the Congress's win in 1946 make the Assembly one-party dominated? Give one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned view is accepted, for example that 208 of 296 seats gave it a clear majority.

questions.q: Draw a bar chart or table of the 1946 results with all ten groups.
questions.a: A chart showing Congress 208, League 73, seven single-seat groups and independents 8.

concepts.name: Table 2.3 and 2.4: communities and women in the Assembly
concepts.description: Community-wise strength of the Assembly and the fifteen women members.
concepts.idea: Hindus were the largest group and fifteen women sat in the Assembly.
concepts.rule: Table 2.3 (296): Hindus 163, Muslims 80, Scheduled Castes 31, Indian Christians 6, Backward Tribes 6, Sikhs 4, Anglo-Indians 3, Parsees 3. Table 2.4 lists 15 women members: Ammu Swaminathan (Madras/General), Annie Mascarene (Travancore and Cochin), Begum Aizaz Rasul (UP/Muslim), Dakshayani Velayudan (Madras), G. Durgabai (Madras), Hansa Mehta (Bombay), Kamla Chaudhri (UP), Leela Ray (West Bengal), Malati Chowdhury (Orissa), Purnima Banerji (UP), Rajkumari Amrit Kaur (Central Provinces and Berar), Renuka Ray (West Bengal), Sarojini Naidu (Bihar), Sucheta Kripalani (UP) and Vijayalakshmi Pandit (UP).
concepts.example: Begum Aizaz Rasul represented the United Provinces (Muslim).

questions.q: Explain what Table 2.3 shows about the representation of minority groups.

questions.q: Compare Hindu and Muslim strengths in the Assembly.
questions.a: Hindus held 163 seats and Muslims 80, so Hindus had about twice as many.

questions.q: Why can the presence of fifteen women be seen as significant in 1946-49?
questions.a: At a time when few women held public office, women from many provinces helped frame the Constitution, showing inclusion of women in nation-building.

questions.q: Was the Assembly's community-wise composition fair? Give one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned view is accepted, for example that it covered many communities but Hindus had the largest share.

questions.a: A table with all fifteen names and correct constituencies.

concepts.name: Table 2.5: membership of the Assembly on 31 December 1947
concepts.description: Provinces and princely states and their members after partition.
concepts.idea: On 31 December 1947 the Assembly had 229 members from provinces and 70 from states.
concepts.rule: Provinces (229): Madras 49, Bombay 21, West Bengal 19, United Provinces 55, East Punjab 12, Bihar 36, C.P. and Berar 17, Assam 8, Orissa 9, Delhi 1, Ajmer-Merwara 1, Coorg 1. Princely states (70) include Alwar 1, Baroda 3, Bhopal 1, Bikaner 1, Cochin 1, Gwalior 4, Indore 1, Jaipur 3, Jodhpur 2, Kolhapur 1, Kotah 1, Mayurbhanj 1, Mysore 7, Patiala 2, Rewa 2, Travancore 6 and Udaipur 2, plus groups such as the Eastern Rajputana States Group 3, Western India States Group 4, and Residuary States Group 4. Total 299.
concepts.example: The United Provinces had the largest provincial membership, 55.

questions.q: What does the strength of the United Provinces and Madras suggest about seat allocation?
questions.a: Seats were allotted roughly by population, so the more populous provinces had larger delegations.

questions.q: Was allotting seats by population a fair method? Give one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned view is accepted, for example that it reflected numbers but gave small units few voices.

concepts.name: Table 2.6: sessions of the Constituent Assembly
concepts.description: Dates and periods of the eleven sessions and the final meeting.
concepts.idea: The Assembly held eleven sessions from December 1946 to November 1949.
concepts.rule: Table 2.6: First Session 9-23 December 1946; Second 20-25 January 1947; Third 28 April-2 May 1947; Fourth 14-31 July 1947; Fifth 14-30 August 1947; Sixth 27 January 1948; Seventh 4 November 1948-8 January 1949; Eighth 16 May-16 June 1949; Ninth 30 July-18 September 1949; Tenth 6-17 October 1949; Eleventh 14-26 November 1949. The Assembly met once more on 24 January 1950 when members signed the Constitution.
concepts.example: The Seventh Session, from 4 November 1948, saw the introduction of the final draft.

questions.q: Explain what the pattern of sessions shows about the Assembly's work.
questions.a: Early sessions dealt with objectives and procedure, later ones with reading of the draft, and the final sessions in 1949 completed the second and third readings.

questions.q: Compare the Seventh and the Sixth sessions in duration.

questions.q: Why did the Assembly meet on 24 January 1950 after the Constitution was passed?
questions.a: So that members could sign the Constitution and it could elect the first President before its commencement on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: Were eleven sessions adequate to make a Constitution? Give one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned view is accepted, for example that long sessions and a second draft allowed careful consideration.

questions.a: A table listing sessions First to Eleventh with correct periods.

concepts.name: Tables 2.7 and 2.8: other constitutions and the concluding Articles
concepts.description: Time taken by framers of other constitutions and Articles 393 to 395.
concepts.idea: The USA framed its Constitution in under four months; Articles 393 to 395 close the Constitution.
concepts.rule: Table 2.7: USA - 7 Articles, 25 May to 17 September 1787, less than 4 months; Canada - 147 Articles, October 1864 to March 1867, about 2 years 6 months; Australia - 128 Articles, March 1891 to 9 July 1900, about 9 years; South Africa - 153 Articles, October 1908 to 20 September 1909, 1 year. Table 2.8: Article 393 short title, 394 commencement, 394A authoritative text in Hindi, 395 repeals.
concepts.example: The American Constitution had only seven Articles.

concepts.name: Experts Committee of the Congress and important facts about the Assembly
concepts.description: The 1946 Experts Committee, its work and other facts on officers and calligraphy.
concepts.idea: The Congress Experts Committee of 1946 prepared material for the Assembly.
concepts.rule: On 8 July 1946 the Congress appointed an Experts Committee under Nehru with M. Asaf Ali, K.M. Munshi, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, K.T. Shah, D.R. Gadgil, Humayun Kabir and K. Santhanam; Krishna Kripalani was co-opted as member and convener. It met in New Delhi (20-22 July 1946) and Bombay (15-17 August 1946), discussed Assembly procedure, committees and a draft resolution on objectives. Granville Austin said it set India on the road to her present Constitution. Other facts: the Assembly's symbol was the elephant; Sir B.N. Rau was constitutional adviser; H.V.R. Iyengar was Secretary; S.N. Mukherjee was chief draftsman; Prem Behari Narain Raizada was calligrapher; Nand Lal Bose and Beohar Rammanohar Sinha decorated it; Vasant Krishan Vaidya did the Hindi calligraphy.
concepts.example: Beohar Rammanohar Sinha illuminated the original Preamble.
